QTIP TRUST (QUALIFIED TERMINABLE INTEREST PROPERTY) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Casey Morgan Lee

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes the legal structure of a "QTIP trust" — a trust holding "qualified terminable interest property" within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7) — as that structure is defined by federal estate-tax law and by the California Probate Code's construction rules for marital deduction gifts (Probate Code §§ 21520-21526). A QTIP trust of this type would typically be created by Jordan Alex Lee for the benefit of Casey Morgan Lee as the income beneficiary, with Jordan Alex Lee acting as trustee and Jordan Alex Lee's children from a prior marriage, in equal shares named to receive whatever remains in the trust after Casey Morgan Lee's death. This sheet states general federal and California statutory rules; it is not a trust instrument, will, or tax election, and it does not itself create, qualify, or fund any trust or make any election on anyone's behalf.

FEDERAL EFFECT OF A QTIP ELECTION: PROPERTY TREATED AS PASSING TO THE SURVIVING SPOUSE
Under federal estate tax law, when an executor makes a valid election with respect to qualified terminable interest property, that property is treated, for purposes of the marital deduction, as passing to the surviving spouse, and no part of it is treated as passing to any other person for purposes of the rule that would otherwise deny the deduction for a terminable interest. This is what allows property held in a QTIP trust — where the surviving spouse receives only an income interest, not outright ownership, and does not control who receives the principal after their death — to qualify for the federal estate tax marital deduction despite the general rule against deducting terminable interests.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "for purposes of subsection (a), such property shall be treated as passing to the surviving spouse, and"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, election with respect to life estate for surviving spouse — general rule (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2056)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(A)(i), the operative "treated as passing" rule. It does not address the mechanics of making the election itself — under § 2056(b)(7)(B)(v) (not quoted here), the election is made by the executor on the federal estate tax return and, once made, is irrevocable. It does not address what happens if no valid election is made (the property then does not qualify for the marital deduction under this provision), the gift-tax analog for lifetime QTIP trusts under 26 U.S.C. § 2523(f), or the separate rule for certain survivor annuities under § 2056(b)(7)(C). It also does not address how California community property or separate property characterization of the transferred property interacts with this federal rule, which was not researched here.

FEDERAL DEFINITION: THE SURVIVING SPOUSE'S "QUALIFYING INCOME INTEREST FOR LIFE"
For property to qualify as "qualified terminable interest property" eligible for a QTIP election, the surviving spouse must have a "qualifying income interest for life" in it. Under federal estate tax law, this requires that the surviving spouse be entitled to all the income from the property, payable at least annually (or have an equivalent usufruct interest for life in the property), and that no one hold a power to appoint any part of the property to anyone other than the surviving spouse during the spouse's lifetime. This is the federal-law counterpart to the mandatory-income and sole-beneficiary features that California's construction statute separately imposes on a marital deduction trust.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "the surviving spouse is entitled to all the income from the property, payable annually or at more frequent intervals, or has a usufruct interest for life in the property, and"
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, definition of "qualifying income interest for life" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2056)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I), the core income-entitlement requirement. It does not address subclause (II) of the same provision (the related no-power-to-appoint-elsewhere requirement, apart from powers exercisable only after the spouse's death), the annuity-treated-as-income rule, the "specific portion" severability rule of § 2056(b)(7)(B)(iv), or any IRS regulations or case law interpreting how strictly or literally the annual-income requirement must be satisfied in a trust's actual administration, none of which were researched here.

FEDERAL RULE: QTIP PROPERTY IS INCLUDED IN THE SURVIVING SPOUSE'S LATER GROSS ESTATE
Property for which a QTIP election was made and the marital deduction was allowed at the first spouse's death is not permanently removed from the transfer-tax system. Federal law includes the value of that property in the surviving spouse's own gross estate when the surviving spouse later dies, because the surviving spouse is treated as having had a "qualifying income interest for life" in it. This is the tradeoff at the center of a QTIP election: the marital deduction defers estate tax at the first spouse's death, but the property (or property later traceable to it) is generally taxed again as part of the surviving spouse's own estate, under the surviving spouse's own estate tax exemption and rates, rather than escaping estate taxation altogether.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The value of the gross estate shall include the value of any property to which this section applies in which the decedent had a qualifying income interest for life."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 2044(a) (Cornell LII text), Internal Revenue Code, inclusion of certain property on which marital deduction was previously allowed — general rule (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/2044)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the general rule of 26 U.S.C. § 2044(a). It does not address § 2044(b), which limits which property this section applies to (property for which a marital deduction was allowed under § 2056(b)(7) or § 2523(f), and only where § 2519 did not already apply to a lifetime disposition of the interest), nor § 2044(c), which treats the included property as "passing from the decedent" for other transfer-tax purposes. It also does not address the surviving spouse's statutory right of reimbursement from the QTIP property for the estate tax attributable to it under 26 U.S.C. § 2207A, or the gift-tax acceleration rule under § 2519 for a lifetime disposition of the income interest, none of which were researched here.

CALIFORNIA CONSTRUCTION RULE: INSTRUMENTS AND FIDUCIARIES MUST BE READ TO PRESERVE THE MARITAL DEDUCTION
California has its own statutory construction rules for an instrument (such as a will or trust) that makes a "marital deduction gift" — defined by statute as a transfer of property intended to qualify for the federal estate or gift tax marital deduction, which includes a gift structured as a QTIP trust. Where such an instrument is governed by California law, its provisions — including any power, duty, or discretionary authority given to a fiduciary such as a trustee — are, by default, construed to comply with the marital deduction provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, and a fiduciary is barred from taking any action or holding any power that would impair the deduction as applied to that gift.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The provisions of the instrument, including any power, duty, or discretionary authority given to a fiduciary, shall be construed to comply with the marital deduction provisions of the Internal Revenue Code."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21522(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), California Probate Code, construction of instruments containing a marital deduction gift (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21522.)
  "The fiduciary shall not take any action or have any power that impairs the deduction as applied to the marital deduction gift."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21522(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), California Probate Code, fiduciary bar on impairing the marital deduction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21522.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21522(a) and (b) only; it does not quote subdivision (c), which separately provides that a marital deduction gift may be satisfied only with property that qualifies for the marital deduction. These are default, gap-filling construction rules: under Probate Code § 21502(a) (not quoted here), this entire statutory part does not apply to an instrument whose own terms, expressly or by necessary implication, make the part inapplicable, so an instrument's actual language can displace what this clause describes. This clause also does not address § 21521, which exempts a trust qualifying as an "estate trust" under 26 C.F.R. § 20.2056(e)-2(b) from two of the related sections in this chapter (§§ 21524 and 21526), or § 21523's separate transitional rule for instruments executed before September 12, 1981, neither of which was researched in detail here.

CALIFORNIA RULE: THE SPOUSE MUST BE THE SOLE INCOME BENEFICIARY, PAID AT LEAST ANNUALLY
For a marital deduction gift made in trust — the structure a QTIP trust uses — California's construction statute imposes two additional default requirements that track the federal "qualifying income interest" rule described elsewhere in this sheet: the transferor's spouse must be the only beneficiary of income or principal of the marital deduction property for as long as the spouse is alive, and the spouse must be entitled to all of the trust's income from that property, paid no less often than annually, for as long as the spouse is alive.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The transferor’s spouse is the only beneficiary of income or principal of the marital deduction property as long as the spouse is alive."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21524(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), California Probate Code, spouse as sole income/principal beneficiary of a marital deduction trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21524.)
  "The transferor’s spouse is entitled to all of the income of the marital deduction property not less frequently than annually, as long as the spouse is alive."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21524(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), California Probate Code, spouse's entitlement to all income at least annually (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21524.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21524(a) and (b) only. It does not quote the balance of § 21524(b), which separately defines how "income" is construed for this purpose (consistent with 26 U.S.C. §§ 2056(b) and 2523(f)) and allows a unitrust payment or other reasonable total-return apportionment to count as income if it meets the requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 643 and its regulations — a distinct and technical accounting question not analyzed here. It also does not address § 21524(a)'s savings clause for a trust that separately qualifies as a "general power of appointment" marital deduction trust, a different (non-QTIP) statutory route to the marital deduction that this sheet does not otherwise cover.

CALIFORNIA RULE: THE SPOUSE MAY REQUIRE UNPRODUCTIVE TRUST PROPERTY TO BE MADE PRODUCTIVE
California's construction statute also gives the transferor's spouse a specific enforcement right connected to the mandatory-income requirement: as long as the spouse is alive, the spouse has the right to require that the trustee of a marital deduction trust make unproductive marital deduction property productive, or convert it into productive property, within a reasonable time. This addresses the practical problem of a trust funded with an asset (such as raw land or non-dividend-paying stock) that generates little or no income, which could otherwise defeat the spouse's statutory entitlement to the trust's income.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The transferor’s spouse has the right to require that the trustee of the trust make unproductive marital deduction property productive or to convert it into productive property within a reasonable time."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21524(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), California Probate Code, spouse's right to require unproductive marital deduction property be made productive (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21524.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21524(c). The source text wraps mid-phrase ("within a" / "reasonable time") purely as an HTML line-wrap in the leginfo.legislature.ca.gov rendering; that wrap was confirmed identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and the quote here normalizes it to a single space with no other change to wording, capitalization, or punctuation. This clause does not define "reasonable time" or "unproductive," does not address what remedy applies if a trustee declines to comply, and does not address how this state-law right interacts with a trustee's duties under the Uniform Prudent Investor Act (covered elsewhere in this corpus) or with the federal "usufruct interest" alternative described in the federal qualifying-income-interest clause of this sheet, none of which were researched here.

CALIFORNIA RULE: FIDUCIARY PROTECTION FOR A GOOD-FAITH ELECTION DECISION
Because the QTIP election is made by an estate's executor (or, for lifetime gifts, by the donor for gift-tax purposes) and is irrevocable once made, California law separately addresses the fiduciary's exposure for that decision: a fiduciary is not liable for a good faith decision to make, or not to make, an election referred to in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7) or § 2523(f).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A fiduciary is not liable for a good faith decision to make any election, or not to make any election, referred to in Section 2056(b)(7) or Section 2523(f) of the Internal Revenue Code."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21526 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), California Probate Code, fiduciary immunity for a good-faith QTIP or gift-tax marital-deduction election decision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21526.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21526 in full but does not define "good faith" for this purpose, does not address what standard of proof or process a fiduciary must satisfy to establish good faith if the decision is later challenged, and does not address a fiduciary's separate potential liability under general trust or probate fiduciary-duty law (such as the duty of impartiality between the income beneficiary and remainder beneficiaries) apart from the election decision itself, none of which was researched here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Alex Lee acknowledges reviewing this information sheet describing the federal and California statutory structure of a QTIP trust — including the federal qualifying-income-interest and second-estate-inclusion rules of 26 U.S.C. §§ 2056(b)(7) and 2044, and the California construction rules of Probate Code §§ 21520-21526 — before taking any further steps toward establishing such a trust for Casey Morgan Lee, with Jordan Alex Lee as trustee and Jordan Alex Lee's children from a prior marriage, in equal shares named to receive the trust property remaining after Casey Morgan Lee's death. This sheet is signed in Oakland, California on September 8, 2026. Prepared by: Jordan T. Reyes.
